architectural_implications.after: Sandbox-owned loop: the model writes a script combining tools such as find_meeting, get_transcript, find_deal, and attach in a single execution.
architectural_implications.before: Host-owned loop: one tool call per turn, sequential round-trips with the orchestrator making branching decisions between turns.
architectural_implications.consequence: Fewer turns and tokens, but the orchestrator loses per-step visibility — observability must move to trace trajectory and execution-level inspection rather than turn-by-turn logs.
architectural_implications.observation: Control flow for multi-step tool use moves from the host agent loop into model-authored code inside the sandbox.

architectural_implications.after: Tool definitions retrieved on demand via search from within the sandbox (progressive disclosure).
architectural_implications.before: All tool definitions pre-loaded into the system prompt, consuming context proportional to integration count.
architectural_implications.consequence: Agents can be wired to far larger integration surfaces at constant context cost, but tool-search quality becomes a new single point of failure and a new thing to evaluate.
architectural_implications.observation: The full tool catalog is no longer a prompt artifact; it becomes a searchable runtime resource.

architectural_implications.after: The agent writes helper functions such as redact_pii() that strip fields before anything reaches context.
architectural_implications.before: Raw API responses flow into the context window; the model is instructed to handle sensitive fields carefully.
architectural_implications.consequence: Enforceable, testable data governance at the runtime boundary; the safety property is reviewable code rather than emergent model compliance.
architectural_implications.observation: Data shaping and redaction shift from prompt instructions to executed code.

architectural_implications.after: Web workers with two-way data binding let the agent drive real browser UI and perform complex UI interactions from within one execution.
architectural_implications.before: One browser action per tool call, each action costing a full model round-trip.
architectural_implications.consequence: Long UI interaction sequences become feasible and cheap, moving browser agents closer to scripted automation with model reasoning at the level of intent.
architectural_implications.observation: Browser/UI automation is driven from inside a code runtime rather than one action per model turn.

article_ideas.angle: Decompose an agent's cost into turn count, per-turn context size, and retries, then show that shrinking per-turn context buys far less than cutting turns — with the 89%-to-2% context and $0.89-to-$0.02 comparison as the worked example.
article_ideas.audience: AI engineers running production agents with multi-API workflows and a token bill
article_ideas.based_on: A quantitative comparison shows code mode cutting token usage 43% and cost 31%
article_ideas.thesis: For multi-API agent workloads the dominant cost lever is eliminating intermediate results from the context window, not model selection or prompt shortening; code mode wins because it converts N sequential prompt round-trips into one program execution that returns only distilled output.
article_ideas.title: Your Agent's Bottleneck Is the Round Trip, Not the Model

article_ideas.angle: Frame progressive disclosure as retrieval-over-capabilities, then examine the consequence the framing is usually used to hide: tool-search quality becomes a new single point of failure and therefore a new thing that must be evaluated.
article_ideas.audience: Agent platform architects and tooling/integration teams
article_ideas.based_on: Progressive disclosure turns tool selection into a retrieval problem

article_ideas.title: Stop Preloading Tools: Capability Discovery Is Just Retrieval

article_ideas.angle: Argue that input validation at the tool boundary no longer covers the blast radius once the model writes arbitrary code, and that safety work migrates from schema design to capability isolation, using API-key exfiltration and unauthorized outbound calls as the threat model.
article_ideas.audience: Security-minded platform engineers and agent infrastructure leads
article_ideas.based_on: the sandbox to be a real security and resource boundary

connections.relationship: Same pattern applied to capabilities instead of knowledge: query at runtime rather than pre-load everything into the prompt.
Environment isolation is the precondition that makes pass-rate comparisons across architectures signal rather than noise.
Moves a policy control from prompt instruction to enforceable, reviewable code at the runtime boundary.
Argues the agent interface should match the modality models were trained on (writing programs) rather than a bespoke JSON tool-call protocol.
Treats telemetry as a queryable dataset the agent can analyze inside its execution environment instead of paging trace data into context.

evidence_quotes.text: Models program the tools inside a sandbox instead of making single API tool calls per turn.
Models can execute multiple tools in one turn, use loops and conditionals, and return only necessary data back to the context window.

core_insights.generalization: Whenever an agent's bottleneck is the number of sequential tool round-trips rather than reasoning quality, moving orchestration into executable code converts N prompt round-trips into one program execution.
core_insights.insight: Code mode relocates tool orchestration from the host's turn loop into LLM-authored code executing inside a sandbox: instead of one API call per turn, the model writes a program that calls several tools with loops and conditionals and returns only the distilled result to the context window.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This changes where the control flow of an agent lives. Turn-by-turn orchestration by the harness becomes in-sandbox program control flow, so intermediate tool outputs never enter the prompt — the primary driver of the reported token and cost reductions.

evidence_quotes.text: Progressive disclosure means models pick and choose only needed tool definitions.
Instead of pre-loading tool definitions into the prompt, code mode gives the model the ability to search and execute tools inside a secure sandbox environment using programming constructs.

core_insights.generalization: Any capability inventory too large to fit (tools, APIs, docs, schemas) should be exposed as searchable/queryable at runtime rather than pre-loaded — the same argument as retrieval over full-corpus prompting, applied to capabilities rather than knowledge.
core_insights.insight: Progressive disclosure turns tool selection into a retrieval problem: the model discovers and pulls only the tool definitions it needs at runtime instead of receiving a full static catalog in the prompt.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Tool catalog size stops being a fixed context tax. Context budget becomes a function of the task rather than the size of the integration surface, which is the difference between supporting 10 and 1,000 tools in one agent.

Writing a Python function `def redact_pii(t):` to remove personally identifiable information before passing it to context.

core_insights.generalization: Placing a code-execution layer between raw data sources and the model context creates a place to enforce redaction, aggregation, and shaping — a stronger control than instructing the model to be careful.
core_insights.insight: Emergent behavior in code mode lets the agent synthesize task-specific helper functions (e.g., redact_pii) that transform data before it reaches the context window, making the sandbox a data-governance boundary rather than only an execution boundary.
core_insights.why_it_matters: PII and sensitive payloads can be filtered or reduced in the runtime instead of relying on prompt instructions not to leak them. It moves a policy concern from soft prompt guidance into enforceable code the agent writes.

core_insights.why_it_matters: It converts the architectural argument into an operating-cost argument: the savings come largely from not carrying tool outputs across turns, not from a cheaper model.

Secret management and over-broad permissions are critical security concerns.

core_insights.generalization: As agents move from constrained API verbs to general-purpose actions, the security perimeter shifts from the tool schema to the runtime; safety work migrates from input validation to capability isolation.
core_insights.insight: Running LLM-written code forces the sandbox to be a real security and resource boundary: CPU/memory ceilings, network egress control, secret management, and narrow permissions are design requirements, not deployment details.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Handing the model a general execution environment vastly enlarges the blast radius relative to typed tool calls. The permissions model and egress policy become core architecture that must be designed before the agent is useful.

Arize Phoenix uses the Harbor framework to run agents through trial permutations, verify outputs using programmatic verifiers, and track success metrics across benchmarks.

core_insights.insight: Isolated per-trial sandboxes make agent evaluations more trustworthy: each trial gets a clean environment and programmatic verifiers check outputs, removing flake and indeterminate behavior from the measurement.
core_insights.why_it_matters: If the environment is reproducible, agent pass rates become comparable across configurations instead of being noise-dominated. That is what allows a pre/post architectural change to be measured at all.

source.title: Stop Giving Your Agent Tools. Give It a Sandbox - Mikyo King, Arize AI

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Mikyo King
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Code Mode: Why AI agents should write and execute code instead of relying purely on traditional tool calling
  • Purpose: To convince AI engineers to transition from traditional multi-turn tool calling to code mode architectures by providing agents with sandboxes and evaluating them effectively using platforms like Arize Phoenix. Mikyo King from Arize AI explores 'code mode', an architectural paradigm where LLM agents are given a programming environment and sandbox to search, compose, and execute tools dynamically rather than receiving a massive static catalog of tool definitions. The talk compares traditional tool calling with code mode, highlighting benefits such as progressive disclosure, composability, token efficiency, and emergent behavior, while also analyzing operational tradeoffs like sandboxing security, resource limits, network egress, and debugging complexity.

Topic Map

The Evolution of Software and Coding Agents

  • Explanation: Software engineering has historically been divided into software for software engineers versus non-engineers. Coding agents blur this boundary by dynamically writing software to solve tasks.
  • Key claims:
    • Software can be segmented into software for engineers and non-engineers.
    • Code mode dissolves the boundary between user interfaces and software by allowing coding agents to build software dynamically.
  • Examples:
    • Extracting invoices from an email inbox via a programmer writing a script versus a non-technical user being restricted by software UI boundaries.
  • Terminology:
    • code mode
    • coding agent
    • software development
  • Why it matters: Foundation models are trained on SWE benchmarks, so aligning agent architecture with code generation enables models to solve problems natively.

The Too Many Tools Problem

  • Explanation: Traditional tool-calling agents suffer from context bloat, token inefficiency, multi-turn latency, and context rot when given large catalogs of tools.
  • Key claims:
    • Giving an agent a huge catalog of tools leads to context window bloat and context rot.
    • Tool outputs that contain junk or require pagination cause multi-turn inefficiencies and increased cost.
  • Examples:
    • Calling CRM, meetings, email, calendar, docs, and tasks APIs sequentially until the context window fills up.
  • Terminology:
    • context window
    • context rot
    • tool definitions
    • tool calling
  • Why it matters: Context bloat increases latency, token cost, and error rates in agentic workflows.

Code Mode Architecture

  • Explanation: Instead of pre-loading tool definitions into the prompt, code mode gives the model the ability to search and execute tools inside a secure sandbox environment using programming constructs.
  • Key claims:
    • Models program the tools inside a sandbox instead of making single API tool calls per turn.
    • Models can execute multiple tools in one turn, use loops and conditionals, and return only necessary data back to the context window.
  • Examples:
    • Writing a Python script combining find_meeting, get_transcript, find_deal, and attach in a single sandbox execution.
  • Terminology:
    • sandbox
    • progressive disclosure
    • composability
    • emergent behavior
  • Why it matters: Code mode dramatically reduces turns, context window usage, latency, and token costs.

Why Code Mode Works

  • Explanation: Code mode leverages progressive disclosure of tools, composability of sub-agents and operations, high token efficiency, and emergent behavior (writing custom tools on the fly).
  • Key claims:
    • Progressive disclosure means models pick and choose only needed tool definitions.
    • Composability allows chaining tool calls sequentially or in parallel.
    • Emergent behavior enables agents to write custom helper functions like redact_pii() to solve complex tasks safely.
  • Examples:
    • Writing a Python function def redact_pii(t): to remove personally identifiable information before passing it to context.
  • Terminology:
    • progressive disclosure
    • composability
    • token efficiency
    • emergent behavior
  • Why it matters: It unlocks advanced reasoning workflows and prevents sensitive data leaks into the context window.

Code Mode in Practice: PXI and Browser Use

  • Explanation: Arize implements code mode in PXI (Phoenix Server) using bash, python execution environments, SQL execution for traces, and browser web workers.
  • Key claims:
    • PXI exposes bash, python execution, and SQLite queries to let agents query traces and manipulate data sets.
    • Web workers with two-way data binding allow agents to drive real browser UI and perform complex UI interactions.
  • Examples:
    • Using executeSQL to query spans in Phoenix or running search_browser_actions in a web worker.
  • Terminology:
    • PXI
    • Phoenix
    • web worker
    • executeSQL
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates practical, production-ready applications of code mode in observability platforms.

Tradeoffs and Open Problems

  • Explanation: Code mode introduces challenges related to resource limits, network egress, secret management, permissions, operational complexity, durability, and determinism.
  • Key claims:
    • LLM-generated code running in sandboxes requires strict CPU, memory, and network egress limits.
    • Secret management and over-broad permissions are critical security concerns.
    • Determinism, handling large binary/image payloads, and smaller model capabilities remain open research problems.
  • Examples:
    • A sandbox running out of memory or an LLM trying to leak API keys or make unauthorized outbound network calls.
  • Terminology:
    • resource limits
    • network egress
    • sandbox
    • durability
    • determinism
  • Why it matters: Engineers must design robust security and guardrails when letting LLMs write and execute arbitrary code.

Evaluating Code Mode with Arize Phoenix

  • Explanation: Arize Phoenix uses the Harbor framework to run agents through trial permutations, verify outputs using programmatic verifiers, and track success metrics across benchmarks.
  • Key claims:
    • Running multi-trial evaluations in isolated sandbox environments eliminates flake and indeterminate behaviors.
    • Code mode reduced token usage by 43% and cost by 31% while maintaining reward and latency in benchmarks.
  • Examples:
    • Comparing pre-code mode vs. post-code mode pass rates across pagedown-root-cause and max-llm-calls tests.
  • Terminology:
    • Phoenix
    • Harbor framework
    • evaluations
    • verifiers
  • Why it matters: Rigorous evaluation allows developers to analyze trace trajectories and tune agent instructions effectively.

Key Points

Context bloat in traditional tool calling

  • Explanation: Providing large catalogs of tools causes context window exhaustion, high costs, and increased latency.
  • Evidence: Comparison graphs showing traditional tool calling consuming 89% context and $0.89 vs code mode consuming 2% context and $0.02.
  • Practical implication: Switching to code mode keeps context clean by returning only necessary execution results.

Emergent behavior and custom tool creation

  • Explanation: Agents can write custom helper functions on the fly to handle tasks that lack pre-built tools.
  • Evidence: Example of an agent writing def redact_pii(t): to sanitize transcripts before passing them to the model.
  • Practical implication: Agents become more flexible and autonomous without needing developers to pre-define every possible tool.

Operational complexity and security risks

  • Explanation: Executing LLM-generated code requires careful sandboxing to manage CPU, memory, network egress, and secrets.
  • Evidence: Discussion on injected READMEs, network egress to malicious domains, and over-broad permission creep.
  • Practical implication: Engineers must implement strict guardrails and isolation layers around agent execution environments.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Code Mode Architecture

  • How it works: The model generates a programming script containing tool calls and logic inside a secure sandbox, executes it, and returns only the final required output to the context window.
  • Components:
    • LLM model
    • Sandbox environment
    • Tool search interface
    • Execution runtime
  • When to use: When building complex agents with numerous tools, high token costs, and multi-turn latency issues.

Harbor Evaluation Framework

  • How it works: Runs agent tasks across multiple trials in isolated sandboxes with network access turned off, using programmatic verifiers to assign binary scores (0 or 1).
  • Components:
    • Task definition
    • Trial sandbox environment
    • Agent under test
    • Phoenix Verifier
  • When to use: When evaluating agent reliability, regression testing, and tuning agent instructions.

Examples & Case Studies

An agent tasked with attaching today's Acme call to the Acme deal in CRM wrote a multi-line script calling find_meeting, get_transcript, find_deal, and attach in one turn.

  • Illustrates: Composability and multi-tool execution in code mode versus sequential single tool calls.
  • Lesson: Code mode allows complex multi-step workflows to execute in a single turn with minimal token overhead.

An agent tasked with removing PXI LLM spans with P95 latency wrote custom Python filtering logic rather than relying on a pre-built filtering tool.

  • Illustrates: Emergent behavior where the agent writes its own utility tool.
  • Lesson: Agents can synthesize specialized solutions on the fly when given programming capabilities.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Give your LLM agents a sandbox and programming execution environment instead of static tool catalogs.
    • Use Arize Phoenix and Harbor for evaluating agent trajectories and running reproducible trials.
  • Strategic:

summary.markdown:
## Overview
- **Speaker**: Mikyo King
- **Channel**: AI Engineer
- **Main topic**: Code Mode: Why AI agents should write and execute code instead of relying purely on traditional tool calling
- **Purpose**: To convince AI engineers to transition from traditional multi-turn tool calling to code mode architectures by providing agents with sandboxes and evaluating them effectively using platforms like Arize Phoenix.
Mikyo King from Arize AI explores 'code mode', an architectural paradigm where LLM agents are given a programming environment and sandbox to search, compose, and execute tools dynamically rather than receiving a massive static catalog of tool definitions. The talk compares traditional tool calling with code mode, highlighting benefits such as progressive disclosure, composability, token efficiency, and emergent behavior, while also analyzing operational tradeoffs like sandboxing security, resource limits, network egress, and debugging complexity.
## Topic Map
### The Evolution of Software and Coding Agents
- **Explanation**: Software engineering has historically been divided into software for software engineers versus non-engineers. Coding agents blur this boundary by dynamically writing software to solve tasks.
- **Key claims**:
  - Software can be segmented into software for engineers and non-engineers.
  - Code mode dissolves the boundary between user interfaces and software by allowing coding agents to build software dynamically.
- **Examples**:
  - Extracting invoices from an email inbox via a programmer writing a script versus a non-technical user being restricted by software UI boundaries.
- **Terminology**:
  - code mode
  - coding agent
  - software development
- **Why it matters**: Foundation models are trained on SWE benchmarks, so aligning agent architecture with code generation enables models to solve problems natively.
### The Too Many Tools Problem
- **Explanation**: Traditional tool-calling agents suffer from context bloat, token inefficiency, multi-turn latency, and context rot when given large catalogs of tools.
- **Key claims**:
  - Giving an agent a huge catalog of tools leads to context window bloat and context rot.
  - Tool outputs that contain junk or require pagination cause multi-turn inefficiencies and increased cost.
- **Examples**:
  - Calling CRM, meetings, email, calendar, docs, and tasks APIs sequentially until the context window fills up.
- **Terminology**:
  - context window
  - context rot
  - tool definitions
  - tool calling
- **Why it matters**: Context bloat increases latency, token cost, and error rates in agentic workflows.
### Code Mode Architecture
- **Explanation**: Instead of pre-loading tool definitions into the prompt, code mode gives the model the ability to search and execute tools inside a secure sandbox environment using programming constructs.
- **Key claims**:
  - Models program the tools inside a sandbox instead of making single API tool calls per turn.
  - Models can execute multiple tools in one turn, use loops and conditionals, and return only necessary data back to the context window.
- **Examples**:
  - Writing a Python script combining find_meeting, get_transcript, find_deal, and attach in a single sandbox execution.
- **Terminology**:
  - sandbox
  - progressive disclosure
  - composability
  - emergent behavior
- **Why it matters**: Code mode dramatically reduces turns, context window usage, latency, and token costs.
### Why Code Mode Works
- **Explanation**: Code mode leverages progressive disclosure of tools, composability of sub-agents and operations, high token efficiency, and emergent behavior (writing custom tools on the fly).
- **Key claims**:
  - Progressive disclosure means models pick and choose only needed tool definitions.
  - Composability allows chaining tool calls sequentially or in parallel.
  - Emergent behavior enables agents to write custom helper functions like redact_pii() to solve complex tasks safely.
- **Examples**:
  - Writing a Python function `def redact_pii(t):` to remove personally identifiable information before passing it to context.
- **Terminology**:
  - progressive disclosure
  - composability
  - token efficiency
  - emergent behavior
- **Why it matters**: It unlocks advanced reasoning workflows and prevents sensitive data leaks into the context window.
### Code Mode in Practice: PXI and Browser Use
- **Explanation**: Arize implements code mode in PXI (Phoenix Server) using bash, python execution environments, SQL execution for traces, and browser web workers.
- **Key claims**:
  - PXI exposes bash, python execution, and SQLite queries to let agents query traces and manipulate data sets.
  - Web workers with two-way data binding allow agents to drive real browser UI and perform complex UI interactions.
- **Examples**:
  - Using `executeSQL` to query spans in Phoenix or running `search_browser_actions` in a web worker.
- **Terminology**:
  - PXI
  - Phoenix
  - web worker
  - executeSQL
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates practical, production-ready applications of code mode in observability platforms.
### Tradeoffs and Open Problems
- **Explanation**: Code mode introduces challenges related to resource limits, network egress, secret management, permissions, operational complexity, durability, and determinism.
- **Key claims**:
  - LLM-generated code running in sandboxes requires strict CPU, memory, and network egress limits.
  - Secret management and over-broad permissions are critical security concerns.
  - Determinism, handling large binary/image payloads, and smaller model capabilities remain open research problems.
- **Examples**:
  - A sandbox running out of memory or an LLM trying to leak API keys or make unauthorized outbound network calls.
- **Terminology**:
  - resource limits
  - network egress
  - sandbox
  - durability
  - determinism
- **Why it matters**: Engineers must design robust security and guardrails when letting LLMs write and execute arbitrary code.
### Evaluating Code Mode with Arize Phoenix
- **Explanation**: Arize Phoenix uses the Harbor framework to run agents through trial permutations, verify outputs using programmatic verifiers, and track success metrics across benchmarks.
- **Key claims**:
  - Running multi-trial evaluations in isolated sandbox environments eliminates flake and indeterminate behaviors.
  - Code mode reduced token usage by 43% and cost by 31% while maintaining reward and latency in benchmarks.
- **Examples**:
  - Comparing pre-code mode vs. post-code mode pass rates across pagedown-root-cause and max-llm-calls tests.
- **Terminology**:
  - Phoenix
  - Harbor framework
  - evaluations
  - verifiers
- **Why it matters**: Rigorous evaluation allows developers to analyze trace trajectories and tune agent instructions effectively.
## Key Points
### Context bloat in traditional tool calling
- **Explanation**: Providing large catalogs of tools causes context window exhaustion, high costs, and increased latency.
- **Evidence**: Comparison graphs showing traditional tool calling consuming 89% context and $0.89 vs code mode consuming 2% context and $0.02.
- **Practical implication**: Switching to code mode keeps context clean by returning only necessary execution results.
### Emergent behavior and custom tool creation
- **Explanation**: Agents can write custom helper functions on the fly to handle tasks that lack pre-built tools.
- **Evidence**: Example of an agent writing `def redact_pii(t):` to sanitize transcripts before passing them to the model.
- **Practical implication**: Agents become more flexible and autonomous without needing developers to pre-define every possible tool.
### Operational complexity and security risks
- **Explanation**: Executing LLM-generated code requires careful sandboxing to manage CPU, memory, network egress, and secrets.
- **Evidence**: Discussion on injected READMEs, network egress to malicious domains, and over-broad permission creep.
- **Practical implication**: Engineers must implement strict guardrails and isolation layers around agent execution environments.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Code Mode Architecture
- **How it works**: The model generates a programming script containing tool calls and logic inside a secure sandbox, executes it, and returns only the final required output to the context window.
- **Components**:
  - LLM model
  - Sandbox environment
  - Tool search interface
  - Execution runtime
- **When to use**: When building complex agents with numerous tools, high token costs, and multi-turn latency issues.
### Harbor Evaluation Framework
- **How it works**: Runs agent tasks across multiple trials in isolated sandboxes with network access turned off, using programmatic verifiers to assign binary scores (0 or 1).
- **Components**:
  - Task definition
  - Trial sandbox environment
  - Agent under test
  - Phoenix Verifier
- **When to use**: When evaluating agent reliability, regression testing, and tuning agent instructions.
## Examples & Case Studies
### An agent tasked with attaching today's Acme call to the Acme deal in CRM wrote a multi-line script calling find_meeting, get_transcript, find_deal, and attach in one turn.
- **Illustrates**: Composability and multi-tool execution in code mode versus sequential single tool calls.
- **Lesson**: Code mode allows complex multi-step workflows to execute in a single turn with minimal token overhead.
### An agent tasked with removing PXI LLM spans with P95 latency wrote custom Python filtering logic rather than relying on a pre-built filtering tool.
- **Illustrates**: Emergent behavior where the agent writes its own utility tool.
- **Lesson**: Agents can synthesize specialized solutions on the fly when given programming capabilities.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Give your LLM agents a sandbox and programming execution environment instead of static tool catalogs.
  - Use Arize Phoenix and Harbor for evaluating agent trajectories and running reproducible trials.
- **Strategic**:
  - Code mode significantly reduces token costs and execution turns while enabling advanced agentic workflows.
  - Security hardening (network egress limits, secret vaulting, permission boundaries) is essential for LLM-generated code execution.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How can we solve durability and checkpointing for long-running code execution steps?
  - What are the best strategies for handling large binary payloads and images inside agent sandboxes without bloating context?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Code mode reduced token usage by 43% and cost by 31% in Arize evaluations. (empirical metric)
- Harbor framework runs trials in isolated sandboxes with network access turned off. (architectural design)
## Notable Quotes
> "Code mode solves a lot of these things. It's kind of an alternative architecture." (at 5:05)
> "Instead of, let's say, just giving it a huge index or a menu of tools, you give it the ability to search for the specific tool and then you also give it the ability to execute the tool." (at 5:10)
> "Give your agent a sandbox. Then evaluate it." (at 23:42)
## Compressed Summary
- Traditional tool calling suffers from context bloat, high token costs, and multi-turn latency.
- Code mode allows models to program tools inside a sandbox using progressive disclosure and composability.
- Benefits include 43% lower token usage, 31% lower cost, and emergent agent behavior.
- Tradeoffs require rigorous handling of sandboxing security, resource limits, network egress, and operational complexity.
- Arize Phoenix and Harbor provide robust frameworks for evaluating and improving coding agents.
- **Keywords**: code mode, sandbox, tool calling, arize phoenix, evaluations
- **Core insight**: Giving agents a sandbox to write and execute code rather than relying on static tool calls drastically reduces token costs and unlocks powerful emergent behaviors.
